_about.what: What Nitzan said in her recorded English takes beyond the script (v19-hybrid), per videoId. 'clean' = her words tidied and math-checked, ready for the AI narration script. keep: yes = carry into the AI script; maybe = optional flavour; no = filler/repeat/wrong. 'slip' flags what she actually said wrong (or a likely whisper error). struggles = spots where the script needs better wording.
_about.source: transcripts/*.json (whisper small.en) aligned with studio v19-hybrid scripts, 8 parallel full reads, 2026-10-11
_about.before_pasting: Before pasting a 'clean' line into an AI script, apply NITZAN_RHYTHM_DELIVERY.md punctuation rules: em-dashes (317 lines) become a comma or a full stop; CAPS stress (24 lines) becomes plain words or the single allowed CAPS word. Use 'to the power of', 'is equal to', 'number three'. Keep numbers different from the Hebrew course (memory: questions-differ-from-hebrew). Old-version takes (q-095, q-096, q-097, q-099, parts of roots) need their numbers re-fitted to the current board.
_about.fields: t = second in her take; type; after_script_line; her_words (near-verbatim); clean; math_ok; slip; keep; why. struggles[] = {t, quote, kind, cause, script_fix}. flow_model = passage worth imitating.

absolute-value.spoken_vs_script: close reading through the rules and sign clues with ~10 additions; big new |-x| example; inequality part re-explained with open/closed range; take ends at 'like x squared', wrap-up skipped

additions.after_script_line: And a distance can't be negative... It's two kilometers.
additions.her_words: And that's why absolute value can always be positive.
additions.clean: And that's why an absolute value is never negative.
additions.slip: Said 'can always be positive', which forgets zero (|0| = 0). Must be 'never negative'.
additions.why: Wrong as said; the script's 'never negative' rule covers it

additions.after_script_line: So with letters, the minus does NOT just drop off. First ask: is the letter positive or negative?
additions.her_words: What happens when let's say we have an absolute value of minus x? ... intuitively, we might think, oh, it's equal to x, because it takes off the negative. But that may not be true, because what if x was negative two? ... Minus minus two is plus, right? The absolute value of just two is two. ... Two is not equal to x, right? Two is equal to minus x ... it doesn't necessarily take off the minus.
additions.clean: And what about the absolute value of minus x? You might think, oh, it's just x, because the bars take off the minus. But what if x is negative 2? Minus negative 2 is plus 2, and the absolute value of 2 is 2. And 2 isn't x, right? It's minus x. So with a letter, the bars don't just take off the minus.
additions.why: New worked example of the classic |-x| trap with letters

additions.after_script_line: Calculate the inside first. Four minus thirteen is negative nine.
additions.her_words: So therefore, I first, I look at this as if it's brackets. So I do four minus 13, which is negative nine.
additions.clean: Treat the bars like brackets: first work out what's inside. 4 minus 13 is negative 9, and only then the bars: 9.
additions.why: Bars-as-brackets is a simple handle for order of operations

additions.after_script_line: What you must NOT do: turn the thirteen positive first and add.
additions.her_words: What a lot of students get mixed up with is, it's not the same as doing ... the absolute value of four and the absolute value of 13. I can't separate them, because then I'll have four plus 13, which is 17. So I have to look at this as one unit
additions.clean: A lot of students mix this up: you can't split it into the absolute value of 4 and the absolute value of 13. That gives 4 plus 13, 17. Four minus 13 is one unit inside the bars.
additions.why: Same content as script, but 'one unit' and 'a lot of students' framing is clearer

additions.after_script_line: Rule three is for a sum.
additions.her_words: When am I not allowed to split them up? In addition, right? In addition, I can't split them up.
additions.clean: So when am I NOT allowed to split the bars? In addition. With a sum, I can't just split them up.
additions.why: Sets rule 3 against rule 2: splitting works for product/quotient, not for sums

additions.after_script_line: Same signs: ... Equal.
additions.her_words: So when we have the same signs, also if they're both positive and also if they're both negative, they'll be equal to each other when I separate the absolute values.
additions.clean: So whenever the signs are the same, both positive or both negative, splitting the bars gives the same result.
additions.why: Makes explicit that both-positive also counts

additions.after_script_line: Absolute value BIGGER than the number? The number is negative.
additions.her_words: It tells me that x is negative, right? Because if it was positive, it wouldn't be greater, it would be the same thing.
additions.clean: Why negative? Because if x were positive, the bars wouldn't make it bigger. It would be the same thing.
additions.why: Gives the reason behind the sign clue

additions.after_script_line: Equal to MINUS the number? Negative — or zero.
additions.her_words: Well, when does absolute value change the sign? So it changes the sign when x is negative, or if it's zero, because adding a minus to a zero, it doesn't do anything, right?
additions.clean: When do the bars change the sign? When x is negative. Or when it's zero, because putting a minus in front of zero doesn't do anything, right?
additions.why: Explains why zero is included in |x| = -x

additions.after_script_line: Two points, one on each side of zero.
additions.her_words: When I have an absolute value is equal to something, I'll always have a negative option it could be, and a positive option to be.
additions.clean: When an absolute value equals a positive number, you always get two options: a positive one and a negative one.
additions.slip: 'Always' is too strong: |x| = 0 has one solution and |x| = negative number has none. Clean version restricts to a positive number.
additions.why: Useful generalisation once restricted

additions.after_script_line: So an equation with bars splits into two cases...
additions.her_words: If I have x minus y is equal to 10 ... I have two options. I have either x minus y is equal to 10, or I have x minus y is equal to negative 10, okay? So I always have two options.
additions.clean: It works with something more complicated too. If x minus y, in bars, equals 10, then x minus y is 10, or x minus y is negative 10. Always two options.
additions.slip: Transcript drops the bars ('x minus y is equal to 10'); she clearly meant |x - y| = 10.
additions.why: Extra example applying the two-case split to an expression with two letters

additions.after_script_line: Two rays, going outward. Open circles — four itself is not bigger than four.
additions.her_words: we basically have here only a certain area that x can't be, right? Basically can't be between negative four and four. It can be everything smaller than negative four, and it can be everything bigger than four.
additions.clean: Look at the number line: there's only one area x can't be in, between negative 4 and 4, and that includes 4 and negative 4 themselves. Everything smaller than negative 4, and everything bigger than 4, works.
additions.slip: She didn't say the endpoints are excluded from the answer; the script's 'open circles' point was skipped. Added to clean.
additions.why: Framing the answer as 'the forbidden middle' is intuitive

additions.after_script_line: Big side: an OPEN range — bigger than the number, or smaller than its minus.
additions.her_words: What I mean by open range, it opens and continues here to an infinite number, and it continues also on this side to an infinite number. There's only a certain range over here that it can't be. ... as opposed to a closed range ... if I say that x is between negative one and one, that's a closed range.
additions.clean: What do I mean by an open range? It keeps going forever on this side, and forever on that side. Only the middle is off limits. A closed range is the opposite: x is between negative 1 and 1, say, and nowhere else.
additions.why: Defines 'open'/'closed range', terms the script uses without explaining

additions.her_words: So x is greater than minus four and smaller than four. That's x, not absolute value of x.
additions.clean: So x is greater than negative 4 and smaller than 4. And notice: that's x itself now, not the absolute value of x.
additions.why: Small but useful reminder that the bars are gone

additions.after_script_line: Rule number one: a sign always belongs to the number right after it.
additions.her_words: a sign always belongs to the number right after it, okay, to the right of it... the minus is attached to the 14 and we're not gonna separate it
additions.clean: A sign always belongs to the number right after it — the one to its right. So this minus is glued to the 14, and we never separate them.

additions.after_script_line: Shortcut: different signs? Take the difference...
additions.her_words: If it's confusing to us to now go into the negatives we could flip both signs instead of doing 9 minus 14 we could do 14 minus 9 and then add the negative right after
additions.clean: If going into the negatives confuses you, flip it: instead of 9 minus 14, do 14 minus 9 — that's 5. Then put the minus back, because the bigger number was the negative one. Negative 5.

additions.after_script_line: Negative six plus four: negative two.
additions.her_words: if this is a bit confusing for you so we could go back to our shortcut... flip both signs and do 6 minus 4... equal to 2 and since we flipped the signs we have to bring back what we flipped... the bigger number was the negative... so this will be negative 2
additions.clean: Confusing? Use our shortcut again. Do 6 minus 4 — that's 2. The 6 is bigger, and it was the negative one, so the answer takes its minus: negative 2.

additions.clean: Both are negative, so we're only moving further left. Do 8 plus 6 — 14 — and the answer is clearly negative: negative 14.
additions.why: mostly the script; adds the 'only going further left' reason for the sign

additions.after_script_line: Big powers? Break the bases into primes.
additions.her_words: If I have, let's say, 27 to the power of four... 27 is three to the power of three, so three to the power of three, all that to the power of four... three times four, so that will give me three to the power of 12

compare-fractions.spoken_vs_script: mostly ad-lib following the beat order; many additions (benchmark idea, extra decimals, 110/111 example, above-one example); several script pieces dropped (above-one extras, root verdict, flip condition, recap)

additions.after_script_line: Think cakes ... / My tip: work from the denominator to the numerator.
additions.her_words: our first technique is to find some benchmark, the benchmark won't always be a half. The benchmark could also be a quarter and comparing to what a quarter of a number would be. In this case it was a half and that differentiates between these two numbers even without knowing what each one of these numbers is on its own
additions.clean: So the technique is: find a benchmark. It won't always be a half, right? It could also be a quarter. Here a half splits the two fractions, without us knowing exactly what either one is.
additions.why: generalises the benchmark idea beyond 1/2

additions.after_script_line: Same numerator — the same cakes...
additions.her_words: the smaller the denominator is the bigger it is because we're splitting up the same piece of pizza, same pie, into less pieces so each piece is going to be bigger. Therefore five of the bigger pieces is going to be bigger than five of the smaller pieces
additions.clean: Same top: the same pie is split into fewer pieces, so each piece is bigger. And five big pieces are more than five small pieces.
additions.why: clear alternative to the kids/cakes picture; script analogy already covers it

additions.after_script_line: Look: five can become fifteen.
additions.her_words: a lot of times we look straight to the denominator. Do I have any way to make eleven match thirty four? Eleven matches thirty three, it doesn't match thirty four... But what can we match? We can match the numerator, the top. And when we match the top we already know how to compare
additions.clean: Most of us look at the bottoms first. Can 11 become 34? No, 11 gets to 33, not 34. So match the tops instead: once the tops match, we already know how to compare.
additions.why: shows the thought process of choosing what to match

additions.after_script_line: Fifty-five, fifty-six. The second is bigger
additions.her_words: And I know that 56 is bigger than 55 and I'm done. That's it. I don't have to find any common denominators, nothing
additions.clean: 56 is bigger than 55, and I'm done. No common denominator, nothing.
additions.why: nice emphasis on the speed of the method

additions.after_script_line: The fix: move the minus sign to the top.
additions.her_words: I'll move it to the top: minus 1 over 2, and then if I compare minus 1 over 2 to a third, I have up here minus 3 and over here 2, and now this is bigger
additions.clean: Let's do it: minus 1 over 2 against 1 third. Cross-multiply: 3 times minus 1 is minus 3, above the first. 2 times 1 is 2, above the second. Now the second is bigger, and that's correct.
additions.why: script states the fix but never runs it; this completes the example

additions.after_script_line: Two negative fractions? Compare them without the minus — then reverse.
additions.her_words: if I had only one number that's negative, that's easy. I don't even have to compare because a negative number is always smaller than any positive number
additions.clean: If only one of them is negative, that's easy. No calculation: a negative number is always smaller than any positive number.
additions.why: script has it as the 'signs first' tip later; good placement here

additions.after_script_line: With the minus, the order reverses.
additions.her_words: 4 times 2 is 8, 3 times 3 is 9. So it would look like this one's bigger, but we're gonna flip it, and therefore minus two-thirds is bigger than minus three quarters
additions.clean: 4 times 2 is 8, 3 times 3 is 9, so without the minus three quarters looks bigger. But we flip it: minus two thirds is bigger than minus three quarters.
additions.why: same as script content

additions.after_script_line: These are the decimals to know by heart.
additions.her_words: now we need to know also how to work with them. We don't want to just memorize this, we want to know also to identify. So if I see let's say three-fifths it should come into mind straight away that it's three times 0.2, which is 0.6. And if I have three over eight, it's three times 0.125, which is 0.375
additions.clean: And don't just memorize them, use them. If you see three fifths, it should come to mind straight away: 3 times 0.2, that's 0.6. Three eighths: 3 times 0.125, that's 0.375.
additions.why: teaches how to build other decimals from the basic ones

additions.after_script_line: [appear] Decimals to know, row 2
additions.her_words: a third is 0.33, a sixth is 0.17, a seventh is 0.14 and a ninth is 0.11. If you're having trouble remembering these I'll remember the first top row and the third with 0.333
additions.clean: A few more worth knowing: a third is about 0.33, a sixth about 0.17, a seventh about 0.14 and a ninth about 0.11. If that's too many, make sure you know the top row, and a third.
additions.slip: values are rounded (1/6=0.1666..., 1/7=0.1428...); last sentence garbled ('the third with 0.333'), probably means 'and one third, 0.333'
additions.why: reads out the row-2 card; script only says it appears

additions.after_script_line: Missing less means bigger.
additions.her_words: When we have two numbers compared and they're both just one from the whole, let's say 110 over 111 and 270 over 271. When they're one apart from each other, then the bigger number is closer to one because the part that it's missing in order for it to be one is much smaller. So this one would be bigger
additions.clean: Here's a rule to take with you. 110 over 111 against 270 over 271: in both, the top is just 1 less than the bottom. The one with the bigger numbers is closer to 1, because the piece it's missing, 1 over 271, is much smaller. So 270 over 271 is bigger.
additions.why: new exam-style example and rule; replaces the dropped above-one example

additions.after_script_line: Zero point six, about zero point six seven ...
additions.her_words: I'm not expecting you to remember any of these decimals. But I want you to remember is that the more we grow by the same number also the top and also the bottom, the larger the number gets
additions.clean: I'm not expecting you to remember these decimals. What I want you to remember: add the same number to the top and the bottom, and the fraction grows.
additions.why: good reassurance and focus

additions.after_script_line: Above one, it goes the other way.
additions.her_words: What happens when the fraction is bigger than one, what we call an improper fraction. So if I have seven over six and two over one. This is an example that makes it very clear. They're both only one above the denominator, but this is actually equal to two, and it's clear that two over one is bigger
additions.clean: Above one, it's the other way. Take 2 over 1 and 7 over 6: in both the top is just 1 above the bottom. 2 over 1 is 2, 7 over 6 is just a bit over 1. So above 1, adding to the top and bottom makes the fraction smaller, it moves down toward 1.
additions.slip: her sentence 'the bigger the number is, the smaller it will be' is unclear; meaning recovered from the example
additions.why: very clear example for the above-1 direction (script's 7/5 vs 8/6 was dropped)

additions.after_script_line: Now it's easy. Cross-multiply: forty-five against forty.

additions.her_words: Now what do I have? I have an equation with only one unknown, only with x's. I don't have any y's left over.
additions.clean: Now I have an equation with only one unknown. No y's left.
additions.why: states the goal of substitution

additions.after_script_line: Back to y equals eleven minus x: y is five.
additions.her_words: Again, what we do is we isolate one letter, plug it into the other one, and we solve it as if we have now one equation with one unknown.
additions.clean: So: isolate one letter, plug it into the other equation, and solve one equation with one unknown.
additions.why: method summary (she skipped finding y = 5 though)

additions.after_script_line: Tip: if they ask for x, isolate y.
additions.her_words: How do I know which one to isolate? Usually there's just one that's a bit easier. If they're asking me for x, we'll isolate y. That way we'll get rid of y. The one that we're isolating is the one that we're getting rid of. But if the question was y equals question mark, we would want to isolate x.
additions.clean: Which letter do I isolate? Often one is just easier. But think about what they ask: the letter you isolate is the letter you get rid of. Asked for x? Isolate y. Asked for y? Isolate x.
additions.why: 'the one you isolate is the one you get rid of' is a crisp rule

additions.after_script_line: Method two — often faster: add or subtract the equations.
additions.her_words: Elimination, and that's something that you probably haven't learned in high school.
additions.clean: Elimination: something you may not have learned in high school.
additions.why: sets expectation; 'probably' may be untrue for many students

additions.after_script_line: Same answer as substitution. Of course.
additions.her_words: So much faster, right? I barely had any steps here. The only thing I needed to recognize is that the y's here would cancel out.
additions.clean: So much faster, right? Barely any steps. All I had to notice is that the y's cancel.
additions.why: sells the method

additions.after_script_line: Same sign instead of opposite signs? Then subtract. The next slide shows how.
additions.her_words: What if the question asks me what y is equal to? I want to get rid of x. If I add, I get 3x, if I subtract, I also get 3x. So I multiply this whole equation by 2 for the x's to match: 2x plus 2y equals 22. Now the x's match, I can subtract. 2x minus 2x disappears, 2y minus negative y is 3y, 22 minus 7 is 15. Divide by 3, y is 5.
additions.clean: What if they ask for y? Then I want to get rid of x. Adding or subtracting won't do it yet. So multiply the first equation by 2: 2x plus 2y equals 22. Now the x's match. Subtract the second equation: 2y minus negative y is 3y, and 22 minus 7 is 15. So 3y equals 15, y is 5.
additions.why: new worked example on the same system; previews 'match coefficients'

additions.after_script_line: Same sign instead of opposite signs? Then subtract.
additions.her_words: How do I know which one I'll subtract from which? I'll take a quick look at the y's. It's much easier to subtract this from this, because then my y's will just be 3y. If I subtract the other way, I'll get into the negatives.
additions.clean: Which one do I subtract from which? Look at the y's: subtract so the result stays positive, 2y minus negative y is 3y. The other way gives negative 3y. Both work, but positives are easier.
additions.why: practical tip, not in script

additions.after_script_line: Same sign instead of opposite signs? Then subtract.
additions.her_words: If they have the same sign, we'll subtract them to get rid of them. If they have different signs, we're going to add them for it to disappear.
additions.clean: Same sign: subtract. Opposite signs: add.
additions.why: clean rule

additions.after_script_line: The shortcut: x is half the sum of the two numbers. y is half the difference.
additions.her_words: There's a small shortcut. If you remember it, it's great. If not, it's not a big deal. When we have this x plus y and x minus y, this is super recurring.
additions.clean: Here's a small shortcut. Remember it, great. If not, no big deal. This pair, x plus y and x minus y, comes up a lot.
additions.why: tells students how much weight to give the shortcut

additions.after_script_line: Every term gets multiplied — including the right side. Six x plus nine y is fifty-seven.
additions.her_words: What's 19 times 3? That's like 10 times 3, which is 30, plus 9 times 3, which is 27. So that's 57.
additions.clean: 19 times 3: 10 times 3 is 30, 9 times 3 is 27. 57.
additions.why: models mental arithmetic

additions.after_script_line: Choose the smallest multipliers you can.
additions.her_words: This is what I do when I have nothing that matches, and I can't even multiply one to get to the other. I multiply both of them to match. These are usually the faster version. The substitution is a bit of high school math. Elimination is what we do in the psychometric usually.
additions.clean: When nothing matches, and one equation alone can't be multiplied to match the other, multiply both. Elimination is usually faster. Substitution is high school math; elimination is what we usually do in the psychometric.
additions.why: contrasts multiplying one vs both equations; method preference

additions.after_script_line: Then adding or subtracting the equations can hand you that combination directly.
additions.her_words: I can't divide this to get x plus y, because if I divide, the ratio between x and y will stay. If I divide this whole thing by 3, this will be x but this will be a third of a y. But what can I do? I can add these up.
additions.clean: Dividing won't give x plus y: if I divide x plus 3y by 3, I get a third x, plus y. The ratio between them stays. But adding the equations gives 4x plus 4y.
additions.slip: she said 'this will be x, but this will be a third of a y' - dividing x + 3y by 3 gives x/3 + y; garbled but the point (ratio stays) is right
additions.why: explains why dividing fails before showing adding

additions.after_script_line: We never found x or y. We did not need them.
additions.her_words: I don't always have to look for what x is individually and what y is individually.
additions.clean: I don't always need x and y separately.
additions.why: repeats script

additions.after_script_line: A product and a quotient. Adding won't help here. But multiplying will.
additions.her_words: This is rare, but it's also useful.
additions.clean: This is rare, but useful.
additions.why: frequency cue

additions.after_script_line: Why do they tell us x and y are positive? Because negative six also squares to thirty-six.
additions.her_words: Now something to notice here: y cannot be zero because it's in the denominator. And denominators cannot be zero.
additions.clean: Notice: y can't be 0 here, because it's in the denominator.
additions.why: condition not in script

additions.after_script_line: Let's lock it in. Which method when?
additions.her_words: Most of this you probably know from high school. The main thing I want you to take from this is the fact that we're allowed to subtract or add different equations. And how do I know which one? It depends what I need. I want to cancel out what I'm not looking for. So always ask yourself, what am I looking for? If I'm looking for x, I need to cancel out y. If I'm looking for y, I want to cancel out x.
additions.clean: The main thing to take from this: you're allowed to add or subtract whole equations. Which one? Cancel out what you're NOT looking for. Always ask yourself: what am I looking for? Want x? Cancel y. Want y? Cancel x.
additions.why: strong closing takeaway
